clue.text: Hilarious joke Planer keeps reeling off

indicators.note: something reeling off staggers away in disorder, so the letters before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A carpenter's plane keeps peeling off shavings like a comedian peeling off jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps' looks like a verb holding something inside, but it is simply part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A knee-slapper is a gag so funny that the listener slaps their thigh while laughing.

clue.text: Poet sleeping quietly once replaced by student

indicators.note: one occurrence of the quiet letter is swapped out for the student letter, and 'once' says only one of the two goes

blocks.note: to kip is British slang for to sleep
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly
L is the learner-driver plate, standing for a student

explanation.surface: A poet who used to sleep quietly has been supplanted by a student.
explanation.walkthrough: KIPPING has two Ps; the second becomes L to give KIPLING.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling wrote famous verse such as If and Gunga Din as well as stories.

clue.text: Increasingly ... or unceasingly

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: more and more
second meaning: for all time, forever

explanation.walkthrough: Split as two words the answer means more and more; run together it means always.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever more says growing steadily greater, while evermore is a poetic word for forever and always.

clue.text: Primarily: son (Eve’s third, happily!)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each following word is kept

explanation.surface: A note on Genesis: Eve's third son arrived, happily, after the tragedy of Cain and Abel.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: in Genesis Seth is the third son of Adam and Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis names Seth as the child born to Adam and Eve after Abel was killed by Cain.

clue.text: Instruments that leave you empty-handed?

blocks.note: surface reading: tools or devices that strip you of possessions, like a robbery
setter's reading: literally nothing in your hands, as when miming a rock guitarist

explanation.walkthrough: Empty-handed usually means coming away with nothing; here it is literal, for the imaginary instruments people strum at gigs.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing these means miming a guitar solo with nothing actually held, purely pretend fretwork.

clue.text: One who went to war with Mexico over a dance

indicators.note: in a down entry, over means the first piece sits above the next one

blocks.clueFragment: One who went to war with Mexico
blocks.note: James K. Polk was the US president during the Mexican–American War of 1846–48

explanation.surface: A president who fought Mexico is seen presiding over a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The war clue points to a US president, not a soldier or general.
explanation.definitionFit: The polka is a lively Bohemian couple dance in two-four time popular since the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Curbs Bahrein’s independence to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A political note: the Gulf state's freedom is partly restricted.
explanation.definitionFit: To rein in is to restrain, like pulling a horse's reins, so curbs is the same verb form.

clue.text: Alarmed as rankest picnic laid out

indicators.note: laid out means set out in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone recoils in horror as the smelliest picnic is spread on the grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a state of sudden terror or fright is exactly what being alarmed means.

clue.text: Beat, in dangerous game, equestrian that’s gutted, jumpy character

indicators.note: something gutted has its insides removed, leaving only its outer letters
in places the first piece inside the remaining pieces

blocks.note: chicken is a game of nerve where the first to swerve loses
to lick someone is to beat them

explanation.surface: A daredevil rider, thrashed in a risky contest, ends up a nervous wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: Chicken Licken is the folk-tale bird who panics that the sky is falling after an acorn drops on its head.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery character is famously panicky, believing an acorn on its head means the sky is collapsing.

clue.text: ‘Samples’ torte (the lion’s share), becomes most rotund

indicators.note: the lion's share is the larger part, so most but not all of these letters are used

blocks.note: the letters run from inside the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone who eats most of a sampled cake grows ever plumper.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the opening S of the first word and take just the T of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample describes a generously large or plump figure; the superlative form means roundest of all.

clue.text: Beer consumed by Doctor Who, essentially an adventurer

indicators.note: something consumed is taken inside, so the beer goes within the doctor word
the essence is the very core, so only the middle letter is taken

blocks.note: to doctor results is to rig them
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: The Time Lord downs a pint before setting off on an adventure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Who' looks like the TV show, but Doctor is a verb meaning fiddle and Who only lends its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Raleigh was an Elizabethan explorer who sailed to the Americas seeking El Dorado.

clue.text: Everyman would back me in France for use of local lingo

indicators.note: to back is to go in the opposite direction, so the French word is read from right to left

explanation.surface: The setter says he would back a Frenchman's use of the local slang.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman's 'I' plus 'd' gives I'D; the French pronoun then reverses to finish.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is an expression or turn of phrase peculiar to a particular language or region.

clue.text: Island producing whisky since – to begin with, and this is not my mistake – ‘190m years ago’

indicators.note: to begin with points to the opening letter of the preceding word

blocks.note: Jura is a Hebridean island with a well-known distillery
sic is printed after a quotation to say the error was in the original

explanation.surface: An island whisky claims, with an odd aside, to have been made since a vastly ancient date.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes and quotation marks dress the clue up as an editorial note; sic is exactly that note.
explanation.definitionFit: The geological period of the dinosaurs ran from about 201 to 145 million years back, which includes that date.

clue.text: Reforms to change open city

indicators.note: to reform something is to reshape it, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Political reforms intended to change a city that is open to the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'Reforms' does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish capital is a major city on the island of Zealand, so city is a fair hypernym.

clue.text: What dentist hates to see and tries to make attractive?

definitions.note: a plural noun phrase, read as two words

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: layers of sugar on teeth
second meaning: makes something unpleasant seem palatable

explanation.surface: A dentist frowns at sweet residue and puts a positive spin on bad news.
explanation.definitionFit: To sugarcoat is to disguise something unpleasant so it seems more agreeable, as with a sweetened pill.

clue.text: Vocally opposed to what poker players do

indicators.note: vocally means spoken out, so the word is taken by its sound

explanation.surface: Someone loudly objects to how card players behave.
explanation.definitionFit: To ante is to put a stake into the pot before cards are dealt, as every player does.

clue.text: Angry about maiden over: bowled, run out – what’s needed when cap’s  not up to the job?

definitions.text: what’s needed when cap’s  not up to the job

indicators.note: about means around, so the angry word wraps the next letters

blocks.note: M marks a maiden over (no runs scored) in cricket scoring
B is bowled on a cricket scorecard
O is a common abbreviation for out

explanation.surface: A cricket scorecard of disaster, then a question about headgear when a cap won't do.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket abbreviations come from scorebooks; in cricket a maiden over is one where no runs are scored.
explanation.definitionFit: A sombrero is a broad-brimmed hat giving far more shade from the sun than a peaked cap.

clue.text: Hilarious character, Judas, perhaps? Not half

indicators.note: not half means one half is dropped, leaving the other

blocks.note: Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus; perhaps signals an example

explanation.surface: Was the infamous betrayer secretly a scream? Not at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The first four letters of the eight go, leaving the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a riot is an idiom for an extremely funny, entertaining person.

clue.text: Stand-alone siesta’s clothing?

indicators.note: clothing means wrapping around, so the answer sits inside these words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: What to wear for a lone afternoon nap.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are wrapped by the clue words, and the whole clue also describes the answer as nap wear.
explanation.definitionFit: A onesie is a single all-in-one garment, comfy enough to wear while napping in the afternoon.

clue.text: Idler and loner we led astray

indicators.note: something led astray wanders off course, so the letters scramble

explanation.surface: A lazy man and a solitary man were led off the straight path.
explanation.definitionFit: A ne'er-do-well is a lazy, irresponsible good-for-nothing who never does well.

clue.text: Part of London not historically associated with aspiration?

definitions.text: Part of London not historically associated with aspiration?

blocks.note: surface reading: an area long seen as lacking ambition
setter's reading: aspiration is sounding an H, which Cockney speech traditionally drops

explanation.walkthrough: Aspiration also means the breathy H sound; Cockneys from this district famously drop their aitches, as in 'ouse for house.
explanation.definitionFit: This district of London east of the City is the traditional home of Cockney speakers.

clue.text: Big cats, not maters for life, we’re told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so sound matters here

blocks.note: those who are unfaithful do not keep one partner for life

explanation.surface: A nature-documentary fact: these big cats do not pair for life.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests animal behaviour; the wordplay is unfaithful partners, said aloud with a non-rhotic accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheetahs are large spotted felines of Africa, the fastest land animals, so big cats fits.

clue.text: Tired, tense author downing whiskey

indicators.note: downing means knocking over, so the whiskey letter is taken out of the author word

blocks.note: to author a book is to write it
W is whiskey in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A weary, anxious novelist knocks back a whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: Author is a verb here, and downing is knocking the W out rather than drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Trite means stale and overused, the sense of tired in a tired old cliché.

clue.text: Introductory – to start with – involved with ABCs?

definitions.text: Introductory – to start with – involved with ABCs?

indicators.note: to start with points at the opening letter of the preceding word
involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed together

explanation.surface: An elementary lesson that is all about learning the alphabet.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue serves as definition too: something concerned with ABCs is elementary.
explanation.definitionFit: Basic means elementary or fundamental, the level at which children first learn letters.

clue.text: Lively, so party regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

explanation.surface: Feeling sprightly, so off to parties as often as possible.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry describes someone active and nimble, especially an older person still full of energy.

clue.text: Making changes, leaving 10 as 500

indicators.note: as here means appearing in the role of, so one number stands in for the other

blocks.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten
D is the Roman numeral for five hundred

explanation.surface: An editor changes a figure in the text from ten to five hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a reference to 10 across, but it is just the number in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Editing a text means revising it, altering and correcting it before publication.

clue.text: Introduce spin: England to give up

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for England

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator introduces a spin bowler as England look set to concede.
explanation.definitionFit: To precede a speaker is to come before them, as when giving an introductory preface.

clue.text: Hairdresser’s newest ‘do’ restyled with dye

indicators.note: restyling hair arranges it differently, so these letters take a new order

explanation.surface: A salon's latest hairdo has been restyled with colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweeney Todd is the murderous barber of Fleet Street from Victorian penny dreadfuls and the musical.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional demon barber is a hair cutter by trade, though with a deadly sideline.
